tagline: Amber coasts, deep forests, rebuilt cities
overview:
Poland lies in the middle of Europe on a broad plain running from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Carpathian Mountains in the south, with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia's Kaliningrad region around its edges. It is about the size of New Mexico.

About 38 million people live in Poland and speak Polish, a Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet and famous for its clusters of consonants. Warsaw, the capital, stands on the Vistula River; its old town was destroyed in World War II and rebuilt brick by brick from old paintings and photographs. Kraków, the former royal capital, kept its medieval squares intact. Poland is a parliamentary republic and joined the European Union in 2004.

The country builds everything from furniture and buses to video games, and its people are known for hearty food, mushroom hunting in autumn, and a deep attachment to their history.
landAndNature: Most of Poland is flat farmland and forest shaped by ice-age glaciers, which also scooped out the thousands of lakes in the Masurian district of the northeast. The Baltic coast has long sand beaches and shifting dunes that creep inland several meters a year in Słowiński National Park, and amber from ancient pine forests washes up on the shore. In the far south the Tatra Mountains, part of the Carpathians, rise to Rysy at 2,499 meters, with alpine meadows and highland shepherds. Białowieża Forest on the Belarusian border is one of the last great lowland forests of Europe, home to several hundred European bison, along with wolves, lynx, and white storks nesting on village rooftops.
peopleAndCulture: Polish meals begin with soup: sour rye żurek, beet barszcz, or chilled chłodnik. Pierogi, half-moon dumplings filled with potato and cheese, meat, or blueberries, appear at every celebration, alongside bigos hunter's stew and pączki doughnuts before Lent. Most Poles are Catholic, and Christmas Eve supper of twelve meatless dishes, eaten when the first star appears, is the year's biggest meal. Chopin's piano music and the poetry of Nobel winners Wisława Szymborska and Czesław Miłosz are national treasures, and the astronomer Copernicus was born in Toruń. Soccer, volleyball, and ski jumping fill stadiums, and speedway motorcycle racing draws bigger crowds here than almost anywhere else.
history: Slavic tribes united under Mieszko I, who accepted Christianity in 966 and founded the Polish state. Joined with Lithuania in 1386, Poland became one of Europe's largest realms, with an elected king and a famously stubborn parliament. Neighboring powers carved it up in the late 1700s, and Poland vanished from the map for 123 years before returning in 1918. Nazi Germany invaded on September 1, 1939, beginning World War II, and the Soviet Union invaded weeks later. The occupation killed about six million Polish citizens, around half of them Jews murdered in the Holocaust at camps including Auschwitz, built on Polish soil. Soviet-backed communist rule followed until the Solidarity trade union helped force free elections in 1989.
funFacts: Warsaw's old town was rebuilt so faithfully after the war that UNESCO lists the reconstruction itself as world heritage.
The Wieliczka salt mine near Kraków holds an underground chapel with chandeliers, altars, and statues carved entirely from rock salt.
Marie Curie, born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, named the element polonium after her homeland.
European bison, once extinct in the wild, were bred back from zoo animals and now roam Białowieża Forest again.
The Crooked Forest near Gryfino has about 400 pine trees that all bend sharply at the base, and nobody is certain why.
